module_title: Understanding Solar Power Basics for African Businesses

lessons.title: How Solar Energy Can Power Your Shop or Workshop
lessons.body: If you run a shop, salon, barbershop, or small workshop in Africa, you know the pain of power cuts. A solar system can keep your business running when the grid fails. Solar panels on your roof capture sunlight and turn it into electricity. That electricity charges batteries during the day, and an inverter converts battery power to the 220V or 240V AC that your tools and appliances use. For example, a small retail shop with 5 LED bulbs (10W each), a fridge (150W), a TV (60W), and a phone charging station (20W) needs about 1.5 kWh per day. A 1.5 kW solar panel array and a 3 kWh battery can cover that. In many African cities, you get 4-5 peak sun hours daily. So a 300W panel produces about 1.2-1.5 kWh per day. To power a workshop with a drill (500W), grinder (800W), and lights, you might need 3-5 kW of panels and a 5-10 kWh battery bank. Start by listing every appliance, its wattage, and how many hours you use it. Multiply watts by hours to get watt-hours, then divide by 1000 for kWh. Add 30% for inefficiencies. That total tells you the size of your solar system. With the right setup, you can run your business without noisy generators or expensive diesel. You will save money, attract more customers who want reliable service, and never miss a sale due to darkness. Solar is not just for rich homes; it is a smart business investment.

lessons.title: Key Components of a Solar System: Panels, Inverters, Batteries
lessons.body: A solar system has four main parts: panels, charge controller, inverter, and batteries. Panels come in two common types: polycrystalline (blue, slightly cheaper) and monocrystalline (black, more efficient in low light). A 300W panel costs about $150-$200 in many African markets. The charge controller regulates power from panels to batteries. Two types: PWM (cheap, less efficient) and MPPT (20-30% more power, worth the extra cost). The inverter changes DC battery power to AC for your appliances. Pure sine wave inverters are best for sensitive electronics like fridges and laptops. Modified sine wave is cheaper but can damage motors. Batteries store energy. Lead-acid (flooded or sealed) are affordable but need maintenance and last 3-5 years. Lithium (LiFePO4) cost more upfront but last 8-10 years and are safer. For a small shop, a 1.5 kW inverter, 2 x 300W panels, a 30A MPPT controller, and a 200Ah lead-acid battery (2.4 kWh) is a common starter kit. Wiring: use thick cables (at least 4mmÂ² for panels to controller, 10mmÂ² for battery to inverter) to avoid voltage drop. Mount panels facing north if you are in the southern hemisphere, or south if in the northern hemisphere. Tilt them at your latitude angle for best sun. Keep panels cleanâdust can cut output by 20%. Always use fuses and circuit breakers. A well-designed system runs quietly and reliably for years.

lessons.title: Calculating Your Daily Energy Needs in kWh
lessons.body: To size your solar system, you must know your daily energy use in kilowatt-hours (kWh). Start by listing every electrical item you use. For each item, find its wattage (printed on a label or in the manual). If only amps and volts are given, multiply them: watts = amps Ã volts. Next, estimate how many hours per day you use each item. Multiply watts by hours to get watt-hours (Wh). Add all watt-hours together, then divide by 1000 to get kWh. For example: 5 LED bulbs (10W) for 6 hours = 300Wh; fridge (150W) running 8 hours (compressor cycles) = 1200Wh; TV (60W) for 4 hours = 240Wh; phone charging (20W) for 3 hours = 60Wh. Total = 1800Wh = 1.8 kWh. Add 30% for system losses (inverter, wiring, battery inefficiency): 1.8 Ã 1.3 = 2.34 kWh. That is your target daily production. Now size your battery: if you want one day of backup, you need a battery bank that can store 2.34 kWh. Lead-acid batteries should not be discharged below 50%, so double that: 4.68 kWh. A 12V 400Ah battery bank gives 4.8 kWh. For panels: in Africa, assume 4 peak sun hours. To produce 2.34 kWh, you need 2.34 / 4 = 0.585 kW = 585W of panels. Round up to 600W (two 300W panels). Use a kill-a-watt meter or a clamp meter to measure actual usage if unsure. Write down your calculationâit will guide every purchase.

lessons.title: Understanding Voltage, Current, and Power in Simple Terms
lessons.body: Think of electricity like water in a pipe. Voltage (V) is the water pressure. Current (A) is the flow rate (how much water moves per second). Power (W) is the total water deliveredâpressure times flow. The formula is: Power = Voltage Ã Current (P = V Ã I). For example, a 12V battery connected to a 10A load gives 120W. If you have a 220V appliance that draws 2A, it uses 440W. In solar systems, you deal with both DC (direct current) and AC (alternating current). Panels and batteries are DC. Inverters change DC to AC. Most African homes and shops use 220-240V AC at 50Hz. Batteries are usually 12V, 24V, or 48V. Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, so you can use thinner cables. For a 1 kW load: at 12V, current = 1000/12 = 83A (very thick cables needed). At 48V, current = 1000/48 = 21A (much thinner). That is why larger systems use 48V battery banks. Always match voltages: a 12V panel must connect to a 12V battery (or via MPPT controller that can handle higher panel voltage). Inverters have a continuous power rating (e.g., 1.5 kW) and a surge rating (e.g., 3 kW for a few seconds) for motor starts. Never exceed the continuous rating. Use a multimeter to check voltage and current. Set it to DC volts to test panels and batteries, AC volts to test inverter output. Clamp meters measure current without breaking the circuit. Understanding these basics prevents mistakes that burn equipment.

lessons.title: Common Solar Myths and Realities in Africa
lessons.body: Myth 1: Solar only works in sunny countries. Reality: Solar works anywhere with daylight, but output depends on sun hours. Africa has excellent sunâmost regions get 4-6 peak sun hours daily, even during rainy season. Myth 2: Solar is too expensive. Reality: Prices have dropped 80% in 10 years. A basic 1.5 kW kit with battery costs $800-$1500, and you can start small and expand. Compare that to a generator: fuel and maintenance cost $50-$100 per month. Solar pays back in 2-3 years. Myth 3: You need a huge battery to run a fridge. Reality: A modern efficient fridge (150W) can run on a 2.4 kWh battery with 600W panels if you manage usage. Myth 4: Solar panels need direct sunlight and stop working when cloudy. Reality: They still produce 10-30% on cloudy days. Myth 5: Inverters are all the same. Reality: Pure sine wave inverters are essential for motors and electronics; modified sine wave can cause buzzing, overheating, and failure. Myth 6: You can connect panels directly to a battery without a controller. Reality: That will overcharge and destroy the battery. Always use a charge controller. Myth 7: Solar requires constant maintenance. Reality: Panels need occasional cleaning; batteries need water checks (lead-acid) every few months. Lithium batteries need almost no maintenance. Myth 8: Solar is only for lighting. Reality: You can run fridges, freezers, power tools, water pumps, and even welding machines with a properly sized system. Myth 9: More panels always mean more power. Reality: Without enough battery storage or an oversized inverter, extra panels are wasted. Balance all components. Myth 10: You can install solar yourself with no training. Reality: Basic DIY is possible for small kits, but wrong wiring causes fires and shocks. Get a qualified technician for anything above 1 kW.

lessons.title: Safety First: Handling Solar Equipment Without Risk
lessons.body: Solar equipment can be dangerous if handled carelessly. Batteries store huge energy and can explode or cause burns. Lead-acid batteries produce hydrogen gas when chargingânever smoke or create sparks nearby. Always charge in a ventilated area. Wear safety glasses and gloves when handling batteries. Acid burns: if acid touches skin, rinse with plenty of water for 15 minutes and seek medical help. Lithium batteries can catch fire if punctured or short-circuited. Use a fire extinguisher rated for electrical fires (Class C) or a lithium-specific extinguisher. Never connect batteries in reverse polarityâit can destroy the inverter and cause sparks. Use a multimeter to check polarity before connecting. Panels produce voltage whenever exposed to light, even if not connected. Cover them with a cloth during installation to prevent shocks. DC voltages from panels can be 100V or moreâtreat them as live. Use insulated tools. Inverters output 220-240V AC, which can kill. Never open an inverter while it is connected to batteries. Wait 5 minutes after disconnecting for capacitors to discharge. Ground your system: connect the inverter case, panel frames, and battery negative to a earth ground rod. Use fuses on all positive cables: between panels and controller, between controller and battery, and between battery and inverter. Size fuses at 1.25 times the expected current. Use proper cable lugs and crimp them tightly. Loose connections overheat and start fires. Keep cables away from walkways and water. Label all wires. If you are unsure, hire a certified solar installer. Do not risk your life or your business. Safety training is not optionalâit is part of the job.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an inverter in a solar system?
options: A) To store energy from the sun
B) To convert DC power from batteries to AC power for appliances
C) To regulate the voltage from solar panels
D) To increase the current from the battery
quiz.explanation: Inverters change direct current (DC) from batteries into alternating current (AC) that most appliances use.

quiz.q: Which component prevents solar panels from overcharging a battery?
quiz.explanation: The charge controller regulates the voltage and current from panels to safely charge the battery.

quiz.q: What does the formula P = V Ã I represent?
options: A) Power equals voltage times current
B) Power equals voltage divided by current
C) Power equals current squared times resistance
D) Power equals voltage plus current
quiz.explanation: Power (in watts) is calculated by multiplying voltage (volts) by current (amps).

quiz.q: If you have a 12V battery and a device drawing 5A, how much power does it use?
quiz.explanation: Power = Voltage Ã Current = 12V Ã 5A = 60W.

quiz.q: Why is a pure sine wave inverter recommended for fridges and motors?
options: A) It is cheaper than modified sine wave
B) It produces cleaner power that prevents overheating and damage
C) It uses less battery power
D) It can work without a battery
quiz.explanation: Pure sine wave inverters output smooth AC similar to grid power, which is safer for sensitive electronics and motors.

quiz.q: What is the first step to calculate your daily energy needs?
options: B) List all appliances and their wattages
quiz.explanation: You must know what you are powering and how much power each item uses before sizing the system.

quiz.q: How many peak sun hours are typically assumed in Africa for solar sizing?
quiz.explanation: Most African regions receive about 4 to 6 peak sun hours per day on average.

quiz.q: What is the recommended depth of discharge for lead-acid batteries to prolong life?
quiz.explanation: Lead-acid batteries should not be discharged below 50% to avoid damage and short lifespan.

quiz.q: Which type of battery lasts longer and requires less maintenance?
quiz.explanation: Lithium LiFePO4 batteries have a longer cycle life (8-10 years) and need no water topping.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fuse in a solar system?
options: B) To protect wires and equipment from overcurrent
D) To convert DC to AC
quiz.explanation: Fuses melt and break the circuit when current exceeds a safe limit, preventing fires and damage.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common solar myth in Africa?
options: A) Solar works in cloudy weather
C) Solar can run a fridge
D) Solar needs a charge controller
quiz.explanation: Many believe solar is unaffordable, but prices have dropped significantly and it can be cheaper than generators.

quiz.q: What happens if you connect solar panels directly to a battery without a charge controller?
options: B) The battery may overcharge and be damaged
C) The panels produce more power
quiz.explanation: Without regulation, panels can overcharge the battery, causing overheating, gassing, and permanent damage.

quiz.q: Why should you cover solar panels during installation?
options: B) To prevent electric shock from live voltage
C) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: Panels generate voltage when exposed to light, so covering them reduces the risk of shock.

quiz.q: What gas is produced by lead-acid batteries during charging that can be explosive?
quiz.explanation: Lead-acid batteries release hydrogen gas, which is flammable and can explode if ignited.

quiz.q: What should you do if battery acid touches your skin?
options: B) Rinse with plenty of water and seek medical help
quiz.explanation: Acid burns require immediate flushing with water for at least 15 minutes and medical attention.

quiz.q: Which tool is best for measuring current without disconnecting the circuit?
quiz.explanation: A clamp meter measures current by clamping around a wire, no need to break the circuit.

quiz.q: What is the typical voltage of a single solar panel used in small systems?
quiz.explanation: Most small solar panels are nominal 12V, though actual voltage can be 18-20V open circuit.

quiz.q: Why is it important to use thick cables between battery and inverter?
options: A) To reduce voltage drop and heat
quiz.explanation: High current at low voltage requires thick cables to minimize resistance, voltage drop, and overheating.

quiz.q: What does a 1.5 kW inverter rating mean?
options: A) It can handle 1.5 kW continuously
B) It can handle 1.5 kW for 1 second
C) It produces 1.5 kW from the sun
quiz.explanation: The continuous rating indicates the power it can supply indefinitely without overheating.

quiz.q: Which of these appliances typically has the highest surge power when starting?
quiz.explanation: Refrigerators have a compressor motor that draws a high surge current for a few seconds on startup.

quiz.q: What is the recommended tilt angle for solar panels in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Tilting panels at your latitude angle maximizes sun exposure throughout the year.

quiz.q: How often should you clean solar panels in dusty African conditions?
options: B) Every few weeks or as needed
quiz.explanation: Dust can reduce output by up to 20%, so regular cleaning every few weeks is recommended.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of an MPPT charge controller over PWM?
options: B) It extracts 20-30% more power from panels
D) It does not need a battery
quiz.explanation: MPPT controllers track the maximum power point of panels, increasing efficiency significantly.

quiz.q: What should you do before opening an inverter for maintenance?
options: A) Disconnect from battery and wait 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: Capacitors inside inverters can hold lethal voltage; disconnect and wait for them to discharge.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a safety practice when handling solar batteries?
options: B) Working in a ventilated area
quiz.explanation: Smoking near lead-acid batteries can ignite hydrogen gas, causing an explosion.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of grounding a solar system?
options: B) To protect against electric shock and lightning
D) To make panels last longer
quiz.explanation: Grounding provides a safe path for fault currents and reduces risk of shock and fire.

quiz.q: If your daily energy need is 2 kWh and you get 4 peak sun hours, what panel size do you need?
quiz.explanation: Panel size = daily kWh / sun hours = 2 / 4 = 0.5 kW = 500W.

quiz.q: Which battery type is best for a business that wants minimal maintenance?
quiz.explanation: Lithium batteries require no water topping and have longer lifespan, ideal for low-maintenance operations.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if a solar panel is cracked?
options: A) Cover it and replace it
quiz.explanation: Cracked panels can cause electrical hazards and reduced output; cover and replace immediately.

quiz.q: Why is it important to match inverter voltage to battery bank voltage?
options: A) To avoid damage and ensure efficient operation
quiz.explanation: Mismatched voltages can destroy the inverter or prevent it from working properly.
